items.title: Anthropic files public S-1 with the SEC for proposed IPO on Nasdaq — ticker 'ANT', H1 2026 revenue $16.3B (≈15× YoY), two customers = 25% of revenue, $80.7B non-cash loss, LTBT codified as Class T directors with Founder-LLC Class F super-voting share
items.summary: Anthropic announced on October 26, 2026 that it has filed a Form S-1 registration statement with the SEC for a proposed initial public offering of Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the ticker 'ANT'. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are lead underwriters. Share count and price range are not yet set. The draft S-1 — reviewed by the Wall Street Journal and summarized by multiple outlets — reports H1 2026 revenue of about $16.3B (Q1 ≈ $4.73B, Q2 ≈ $11.5B), up from about $1.1B in H1 2025 — roughly a 15× year-over-year jump. Reported H1 2026 net loss is $80.7B, overwhelmingly a non-cash charge tied to re-valuation of convertible financing instruments as the company's implied valuation climbed; adjusted operating income is reported positive for the quarter per Bloomberg. Two unnamed customers accounted for about 25% of H1 revenue; Amazon and Google marketplaces together generated roughly 47% of 2025 revenue, highlighting significant channel concentration. Cited compute commitments range from $518B (one report) to more than $600B, with up to $750B when deals under negotiation are included. The S-1 formalizes a three-class share structure: Class A (public), Class T (held by the Long-Term Benefit Trust — no economic rights; the trust elects and removes the Class T directors, who will constitute a majority of the board), and a single share of Class F common stock issued to the Founder LLC immediately prior to the offering, entitled to 50.1% of total voting power on certain matters. Anthropic will remain a Delaware Public Benefit Corporation. Secondary coverage ties the filing to the Series H that raised $65B at a $965B post-money valuation and reports target IPO valuation in the ~$2T range for a November listing; the public prospectus is now on EDGAR (anthropicpbc-sx1.htm).
items.why_it_matters: This is the single most consequential governance and financial event in Anthropic's history, and it closes the loop on three stories the agent has been tracking across the past week: the Stubbs appointment to the LTBT (Oct 21, in today's am file), the Public Benefit Fund (Oct 18), and now the S-1 itself. The three items are not independent — they are the sequence of pre-IPO moves that collectively lock in the governance structure Anthropic plans to carry into public markets. What the S-1 reveals that was not previously public: (1) the LTBT is codified as the elector of a majority of the board via Class T stock — not an advisory committee but a legally binding mechanism; (2) the Founder LLC gets 50.1% voting power on certain matters via a single Class F share — the SpaceX / Snap / Google founder-control playbook, with an explicit twist that the founder super-vote and the LTBT board-election power coexist, so the trust can still pick the directors even while founders hold voting control on specified matters; (3) the PBC status is preserved rather than converted, which means fiduciary duty requires balancing shareholder pecuniary interests, the interests of those materially affected by the company, and the stated public benefit purpose. The financials are the other half of the story: ≈15× YoY revenue growth is at a scale that very few operating companies have achieved at this valuation level, but customer concentration (two customers = 25% of H1 revenue, Amazon + Google marketplaces = 47% of 2025 revenue) is the specific risk factor every reader of the eventual public S-1 will underline. The $80.7B 'loss' is a non-cash accounting artifact of the convertible financing round, not a cash burn number — distinguishing the two is going to be the central interpretive battle in press coverage over the next three weeks. The compute commitments ($518B–$600B+, up to $750B including deals in negotiation) are the number that matters for understanding why the company needs public-market capital: Anthropic is pre-committing to compute spend at a scale that no amount of private financing can plausibly cover, which is itself the operational reason for the IPO. For Gabe, the direct relevance is twofold: (1) the SKILL.md format he interacts with every day inside Claude Code is now a product of a company that is about to be scrutinized by the SEC, equity analysts, and shareholders — the model-safety-vs-shareholder-return tension is no longer theoretical, it is a Delaware fiduciary-duty question embedded in a PBC charter he can go read on EDGAR; (2) the LTBT item in his am file today was effectively the pre-game of this filing, so the governance-structure items the agent has been surfacing this week stack together into a complete picture rather than three separate curiosities. The honest caveats: (a) press figures do not all agree — H1 revenue cited ranges from $16.3B to a disputed $16.8B Q3-only number from one outlet; compute commitments span $518B–$750B depending on which deals are counted; valuation targets ($2T) are from secondary reporting, not the filing itself; (b) the Delaware PBC fiduciary-duty structure is a plausible target for post-IPO shareholder litigation, and no company at Anthropic's scale has yet had its PBC commitments tested in Chancery Court; (c) the Class F super-vote has a specified set of matters it applies to — the exact perimeter of that set, as written in the filing, is the piece worth reading in the full text when it clears SEC review and becomes effective; (d) one Chinese-language cite in secondary coverage described the structure as 'Class B / Class T', which conflicts with the S-1's own 'Class A / Class T / Class F' naming, so trust the filing over the aggregator write-ups. The piece to watch over the next three weeks: pricing. Any pricing above the Series H's $965B is a public-market endorsement of the trust/founder-share governance structure; pricing below is the first market pushback on a PBC's ability to carry mission commitments through public listing — the exact test the governance-focused readers have been waiting for since Anthropic incorporated as a PBC.
items.why_it_matters_brief: Anthropic's public S-1 lands with Nasdaq ticker 'ANT', ≈$16.3B H1 revenue (≈15× YoY), two customers at 25% of revenue, and a Class A/T/F structure that codifies the LTBT's board-election power alongside a 50.1% founder super-vote — the governance test for a PBC under public-market scrutiny begins now.

items.title: Mistral Large 4 open weights expected October 27 — 1.05T total / 49B active MoE, 1M context, custom license (not Apache 2.0 like Large 3), early access currently gated to developers, cybersecurity firms, and governments
items.summary: Mistral AI opened a public preview of Mistral Large 4 on October 6, 2026, with the full open-weights release planned for 'end of October' — one outlet (Forklog) specifies October 27, 2026 as the planned date, which if accurate is tomorrow. The model's documentation lists approximately 1.05 trillion total parameters with around 49 billion active per query under a mixture-of-experts arrangement, plus a separate 1.6 billion-parameter vision encoder. Mistral's docs quote a 1 million token context window; third-party tracker Vals AI's listing shows 512k, so the real deployed context is still worth confirming on release. Current preview access is a hosted API through Mistral Studio. Mistral has stated the open-weights checkpoint will ship under a custom license — a departure from Large 3's Apache 2.0. Until the weights land, Mistral is giving early access to developers, cybersecurity specialists, and government organizations; a separate private API with reduced moderation is reportedly available to 'privileged' partners including cybersecurity firms and state authorities. Benchmark figures so far come from Mistral and are preliminary; Vals AI's independent Vals Index ranks Mistral Large 4 at #32 of 44 models with a 48.05% score. One secondary summary cites a 52B-active figure vs the more commonly reported 49B — treat the active-parameter count as 49B until the weights land and config files can be read.
items.why_it_matters: Mistral is the largest European lab still releasing open-weight frontier models at a competitive scale, and Large 4 is the piece of the Oct 2026 open-weights race that has been publicly committed to but not yet shipped — if the Oct 27 date holds, this is a Tier-1 story tomorrow. Three specifics worth tracking before the weights land: (1) the custom-license departure from Apache 2.0 is the material story — Large 3 was broadly reusable under permissive terms, and a custom license on a trillion-parameter MoE will meaningfully shape who can self-host, redistribute, or build commercial products on top; (2) the 1M vs 512k context discrepancy between Mistral's own docs and Vals AI's listing is the kind of fact that the weights release will settle definitively, so the config.json in the HuggingFace drop is the thing to read on arrival; (3) the private-API-with-reduced-moderation channel reportedly offered to cybersecurity firms and state authorities is a two-track safeguards story — relaxed safeguards for government and cybersec reads similar to Anthropic's LSVP tier for life-sciences orgs, but the perimeter is wider (not just one domain) and the licensing arrangement less visible, so the governance watchers will be comparing those two tiering programs directly. For Gabe: he does not need to run a 1T-parameter MoE locally — nobody with normal hardware does — but the arrival of a non-Apache-licensed trillion-parameter checkpoint on Hugging Face still matters because it fixes the ceiling for what a European open-weight release looks like under current competitive pressure, and because the smaller Mistral derivatives (if any ship this cycle) will be the ones that could run on consumer-grade hardware or appear quickly in Ollama. The honest caveats: (a) the Oct 27 date is from a single secondary source (Forklog) — Mistral's own announcement only commits to 'end of October'; (b) all current benchmarks are Mistral-run and preliminary, and the Vals Index placement at #32/44 is strikingly weak for a trillion-parameter model, so independent evaluations after the weights land are the thing to watch; (c) the 49B vs 52B active-parameter discrepancy is small but matters for inference-cost math, since active-params × context dominates throughput costs on MoE serving. The piece to watch tomorrow: whether the custom license is permissive enough for commercial fine-tuning and redistribution, or whether it introduces the kind of 'you can download but not actually use at scale' constraint that gated Llama 2's early days — that distinction will decide whether Large 4 becomes the European open-weights ecosystem's anchor model or a technically-impressive but practically-constrained reference release.
